lessons.title: Commodities, Collectibles and Crypto: Returns Without Cash Flows

children.text: A share of Infosys pays dividends from profits. A bond pays interest. A flat pays rent. Now consider a barrel of crude oil, a painting by M.F. Husain and a bitcoin. None of them pays you anything while you hold it. Their entire return comes from someone paying more for them later. That one fact reshapes everything about their risk and return: there is no income to fall back on, no cash flow to anchor a fair price, and nothing but the next buyer's willingness to pay. This lesson profiles the three main families of cash-flowless alternatives and shows why they need to be sized very differently from everything else in your portfolio.

body.text: When an asset produces no cash flows, its price is whatever the next buyer will pay. That makes returns possible without any underlying growth, and losses possible without any underlying damage. Size these assets for how far they can fall, not for how far they have risen.

children.text: Chapter 3 treated gold as a traditional benchmark because of its long history as money and its crisis record. The assets in this lesson share gold's lack of income but not that history, and that is exactly why their swings are so much larger.

children.text: Crude oil, natural gas, copper, aluminium, silver and agricultural products are consumed, not held for income. Their prices follow supply and demand, which move in long cycles: high prices encourage new supply, which eventually pushes prices down again. Over long periods, many commodities have struggled to beat inflation on price alone. Indian investors can get exposure through futures on MCX, and for silver through silver ETFs, which have been available since 2022.
The hidden cost of holding commodities through futures

markDefs.definition: A market where futures contracts for later months trade above the current price, often because of storage and financing costs. Rolling from one contract to the next then costs money.

children.text: Most people cannot store barrels of oil, so they hold futures contracts and replace, or roll, them before they expire. When later contracts cost more than the expiring one, a situation called
, every roll means selling low and buying high. You can lose money even if the commodity's price does not change at all.

body.caption: Assumes the spot price stays flat and each monthly roll has the same gap

body.title: Losing money on a flat price
body.prompt: Crude oil's price stays flat all year. Each month, an investor sells the expiring futures contract at ₹100 and buys the next month's contract at ₹101. After 12 monthly rolls, roughly what percentage of value has the investor lost? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Each roll keeps 100 ÷ 101 of the value. After 12 rolls: (100 ÷ 101)^12 ≈ 0.887, a loss of about 11.3%, with no change in the oil price. With a ₹2 gap each month, the loss would be about 21%. This is why commodity funds can badly lag the commodity itself.

children.text: 2. Collectibles and Art: Scarcity, Taste and Very High Costs

Indian art has produced headline-grabbing auction prices in recent years, with works by artists such as Amrita Sher-Gil, S.H. Raza and M.F. Husain selling for tens of crores. Watches, rare coins, stamps and vintage cars have their own devoted markets. Headlines, though, come from the very top of a market where most pieces sell for far less, or do not sell at all. Collectibles carry the full set of alternative traits from Chapter 1 in their most extreme form.

cells: Auction houses commonly charge buyers a premium and sellers a commission, which together can take 25% or more of the price, plus GST
Every piece is unique, so value is an estimate until it sells; returns data suffers badly from survivorship bias
Selling depends on finding the right buyer, often only at specific auctions
Forgeries, disputed provenance or damage can destroy value
Insurance, secure storage and conservation, with no income to pay for them
Fashions change, and an artist or category can fall out of favour for decades

body.text: Collectibles can deliver a real return that is not financial: the enjoyment of owning a painting or a watch you love. That is a legitimate reason to buy. It is not a reason to count them as a core investment, and it is worth being honest with yourself about which one you are doing.

children.text: 3. Crypto Assets: Extreme Volatility, Heavy Tax, Custody Risk

markDefs.definition: The term used in Indian income tax law for crypto assets and similar tokens, taxed under a special regime since April 2022.

children.text: Bitcoin, Ethereum and other tokens are the newest cash-flowless asset. Their prices rest on adoption and belief in the network, and they have delivered both spectacular gains and repeated falls of 75% or more. In India, they are taxed as
under one of the harshest regimes of any asset class.

body.caption: How crypto gains are taxed in India, compared with listed equity

cells: Flat 30%, plus surcharge and cess, regardless of holding period
Only the cost of acquisition; no expenses
Cost of acquisition and transfer expenses
Cannot be set off against other gains or carried forward
Can be set off and carried forward under the rules
None for resident investors on listed shares

body.title: Show me why the loss rule hurts so much

children.text: Suppose in one year you make a ₹1 lakh gain on bitcoin and a ₹1 lakh loss on another token. Overall, you made nothing. But because crypto losses cannot be set off against gains, you still owe 30% tax on the ₹1 lakh gain: ₹30,000, plus cess. You paid tax on a year in which you earned zero. With listed equity, the loss would have offset the gain.

Crypto also adds a risk the other assets in this course mostly do not: custody and platform risk. If the exchange or wallet holding your tokens fails or is hacked, you can lose assets regardless of what the market does.

children.text: Because these assets can fall 75 to 85% without any income to cushion the blow, size them by the damage a severe fall would do to your whole portfolio.

body.title: The missing anchor
body.question: Why can a crypto token or a collectible fall 80% without anything being "wrong" with it, while a profitable company's share is less likely to fall that far for long?
options: Because tokens and collectibles are always frauds
Because they produce no cash flows, so there is no income to anchor their price when buyers lose interest
Because volatility only affects assets bought online
body.explanation: A profitable company keeps earning, and eventually investors value those earnings. An asset with no cash flows has no such floor: its price depends entirely on what the next buyer will pay, which can drop sharply and stay low for years.

body.title: Name the futures market condition
body.textWithBlank: When later-month futures contracts trade above the current price, so that rolling contracts forward costs money, the market is said to be in ___.
body.explanation: Contango is common in commodities like crude oil, where storage costs money. It is the main reason commodity funds that roll futures can lag the commodity price for years.

body.title: Aditya's crypto plan
body.scenario: Aditya, 26, a software engineer in Hyderabad, has ₹8 lakh saved: ₹5 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund and ₹3 lakh in an FD for emergencies. After watching bitcoin rally, he plans to move half his savings, ₹4 lakh, into crypto on an exchange app, including part of his emergency FD. He says: "I am young, so I can take the risk."
body.prompt: Apply the ideas in this lesson. What is wrong with the plan, and what might a more sensible approach look like?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Size of the fall: bitcoin has fallen about 77 to 84% in past cycles. At 50% of his savings, a 77% fall would cost about ₹3.08 lakh, or 38.5% of everything he has.

2. Recovery math: after a 77% fall, the asset needs to rise about 335% just to get back. Being young gives him time, but not certainty of recovery.

3. Emergency fund: using part of his FD means a job loss or medical bill during a crash would force him to sell at a deep loss. Risk tolerance is not only about age; it is about whether he can avoid selling.

4. Tax: gains are taxed at a flat 30% plus cess, and losses cannot be set off or carried forward, so a mix of winners and losers can leave him paying tax on no net gain.

5. Custody risk: exchange failures and hacks, from FTX to WazirX, have frozen or wiped out customer holdings regardless of price.

A more sensible approach: keep the ₹3 lakh emergency fund intact, keep the index fund as the core, and cap crypto at a small share he could lose completely without changing his life, perhaps 5% of savings, or about ₹40,000. A 77% fall would then cost about ₹30,800, under 4% of his savings. He should use a FIU-registered exchange and add to it only from new savings, not existing safety money.

points: Commodities, collectibles and crypto produce no cash flows, so their price is whatever the next buyer will pay, with no income to anchor it.
Their swings are far larger than equity: illustrative volatility runs from about 25% for silver to about 65% for bitcoin, against about 18% for the Nifty.
Commodities move in supply-and-demand cycles, and contango can cost futures holders around 11% a year even when prices are flat.
Collectibles carry very high transaction costs, unique-item valuation, authenticity risk and taste risk, and their returns data is heavily skewed by survivorship.
Crypto adds a harsh Indian tax regime of flat 30%, no loss set-off and 1% TDS, plus custody and platform risk.
Size cash-flowless assets by the damage a 75 to 85% fall would do: a 5% allocation loses under 4%, while a 50% allocation loses nearly 40%.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any commodity, collectible or crypto asset. Crypto assets are not regulated as securities in India and can lose most or all of their value. Volatility figures and price moves are approximate and illustrative. Tax rules can change. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before making decisions.
